title: Your first end-to-end RAG in 100 lines
summary: A complete retrieval pipeline with no dependencies, assembled from the last five days. Then two real failures traced to their exact cause: an off-topic query whose whole vector collapses to the word 'of', and a correct answer that ranks fourth because IDF measures rarity rather than meaning.
html:
Seven days of parts. Today they become one program. No libraries, nothing imported that you have not already understood, and the whole retrieval half of RAG in about a hundred lines.

Then you are going to run it and watch it fail twice, in two different ways, and those two failures are the actual lesson.

The code

Chunking, from Day 6. Fixed windows with overlap, stride is size minus overlap:

import math, re
from collections import Counter

def chunk(text, size=120, overlap=20):
    words, stride, out = text.split(), size - overlap, []
    for start in range(0, max(len(words) - overlap, 1), stride):
        piece = words[start:start + size]
        if piece:
            out.append(" ".join(piece))
    return out

The index, which is Days 3, 4 and 5 together. Note df counts over set(doc), documents and not occurrences, which is the bug you were warned about:

def tokenize(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())

class Index:
    def __init__(self, chunks):
        self.chunks = chunks
        toks = [tokenize(c) for c in chunks]
        n = len(chunks)
        df = Counter(t for doc in toks for t in set(doc))
        self.idf = {t: math.log(n / d) for t, d in df.items()}
        self.vectors = [self._weight(Counter(doc)) for doc in toks]

    def _weight(self, counts):
        vec = {}
        for term, c in counts.items():
            idf = self.idf.get(term)
            if idf:
                vec[term] = (1 + math.log(c)) * idf
        return normalize(vec)

    def embed(self, text):
        return self._weight(Counter(tokenize(text)))

    def search(self, question, k=3):
        q = self.embed(question)
        scored = [(dot(q, v), i) for i, v in enumerate(self.vectors)]
        scored.sort(reverse=True)
        return [(s, i, self.chunks[i]) for s, i in scored[:k] if s > 0]

def normalize(vec):
    mag = math.sqrt(sum(w * w for w in vec.values()))
    return {t: w / mag for t, w in vec.items()} if mag else vec

def dot(a, b):
    if len(a) > len(b):
        a, b = b, a
    return sum(w * b.get(t, 0.0) for t, w in a.items())

Normalising at build time means search is a plain dot product, exactly the optimisation from Day 5. Then prompt assembly, which is the string concatenation from Day 1:

SYSTEM = ("Answer the question using only the context below.\n"
          "If the context does not contain the answer, say so.")

def build_prompt(question, hits):
    ctx = "\n\n".join(f"[{i+1}] {t}" for i, (_, _, t) in enumerate(hits))
    return f"{SYSTEM}\n\n<context>\n{ctx}\n</context>\n\nQuestion: {question}"

That is the system. Point it at a document, ask a question, get ranked chunks and a finished prompt. Send that string to any model and you have RAG.

Running it

I ran this over six paragraphs about honeybees, which chunked into 5 chunks and 270 vocabulary terms. The easy question works:

Q: who lays the eggs?
   0.200  chunk 0: A honeybee colony is a single reproductive unit...

Correct chunk, top rank. The queen paragraph. Everything you built does what it was supposed to.

Failure one: it answers a question it has no business answering

Q: what is the boiling point of mercury?
   0.057  chunk 4: Communication inside the dark hive is mechanical...
   0.032  chunk 3: a supersaturated sugar solution with too little...

There is nothing about mercury in this corpus. The system returned three chunks anyway, with positive scores. Here is why, and it is worth tracing exactly:

  • boiling, point, mercury are not in the vocabulary. self.idf.get(term) returns None and they are silently dropped.
  • what, is, the appear in every chunk, so their IDF is exactly 0 and they contribute nothing.
  • of appears in most but not all chunks, so its IDF is 0.223. It survives.

After weighting, the entire query vector is {"of": 1.0}. The ranking you are looking at is which chunk contains the most instances of the word "of". The system has no concept of "nothing here is relevant", because a dot product of two non-negative vectors is either positive or zero, and there is no threshold that means no.

This is the refusal path from Day 1, and you now know it has to be built deliberately. It does not fall out of the retrieval math. Day 65 covers doing it properly.

Failure two: the right answer comes fourth

Ask how bees make honey. The best paragraph in the corpus is the one about ripening, nectar at eighty percent water dried down to under eighteen, capped when yeasts can no longer grow. That is chunk 3. Here is the full ranking:

chunk 1: 0.150   worker job stages
chunk 2: 0.099   foraging and invertase
chunk 0: 0.048   colony castes
chunk 3: 0.011   ripening and dehydration      <- the actual answer
chunk 4: 0.000   waggle dance

Fourth out of five, and at k=3 it never reaches the model at all. The query vector explains it:

how: 0.756    do: 0.430    honey: 0.430    bees: 0.240
(make: dropped, not in vocabulary)

The word how carries 0.756 of the query's weight. It is a function word with no topical content whatsoever, and it dominates because it happens to be rare in this corpus. IDF measures rarity. It does not measure meaningfulness, and in a small corpus those two come apart badly. Meanwhile make, a real content word, was dropped entirely for never appearing.

The deeper problem is the one from Day 3 that has been open ever since. Chunk 3 is about honey production and says so using the words ripening, dehydration, nectar and water. The query says make. There is no lexical overlap on the concept, so no amount of weighting will rescue it.

Everything you have built compares surface forms. It has never once compared meaning.

The third problem, which is not a failure yet

Look at search again. It builds a score for every vector in the index, then sorts. That is a linear scan, and at five chunks it is free.

At a million chunks it is a million dot products per query, plus a sort over a million scores, on every single question. Rough arithmetic: a five term query doing one dictionary lookup per chunk is five million lookups, which in Python is a few hundred milliseconds of pure overhead before any real work. You can move it to C and win maybe fifty times, and it is still linear. Double your corpus and you double your query latency, forever.

The interesting part is that for this particular scorer, the linear scan is not just slow, it is unnecessary. Most chunks share zero terms with the query and score exactly 0. You computed them anyway. Day 3 gave you the structure that fixes it: store the index column major, term to list of chunks, and you visit only the chunks that contain a query term. That is an inverted index, and it is why lexical search has scaled to the entire web since the 1990s.

Dense vectors from Day 9 onward do not have that escape, because every dimension is non-zero and every chunk genuinely does have a score. That is what makes approximate nearest neighbour search necessary, and it is the whole of Phase 2 starting on Day 15.

What you actually have

A working retrieval system, honestly evaluated, that fails in precisely the two ways this course spends the next ninety days fixing. Keep this file. On Day 14 you will measure it properly and get a baseline number, and from Day 9 onward you will start replacing pieces of it.

Tomorrow you replace the biggest piece. Neural embeddings, and what a transformer encoder does that a word count cannot.
exercise:
1. Run it on your own corpus. Paste the code together, point it at a directory of your own documents (concatenate them, or index each file as a chunk source), and ask it five real questions you know the answers to. Write down how many of the five put the correct chunk at rank 1.

2. Find your own "of". Add two lines to print the query vector after weighting: q = idx.embed(question); print(sorted(q.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:5]). Ask an off-topic question and look at what survives. Every corpus has a term that behaves like of did here, and knowing yours tells you something about your vocabulary.

3. Try to fix failure two without neural embeddings. Give it ten minutes. Add a stopword list, or floor the IDF, or drop query terms below a weight threshold. See how far you get. The point is to feel where the ceiling is, because tomorrow's lesson is about going through it rather than under it.
